screens.title: OSPF Route Summarization and Virtual Links
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn two scalable OSPF techniques: route summarization to keep routing tables compact and virtual links to temporarily reconnect an isolated area to the backbone. We'll show why summarization reduces memory and SPF work, how ABRs and ASBRs perform different summarization roles, and how a Junos ABR uses area-range to advertise a single Type 3 summary instead of multiple specific networks. Then we'll examine virtual links: what they are, when they are acceptable, and how to configure them by specifying the neighbor Router IDs and the transit area. You will see concrete Junos configuration examples and verification commands that demonstrate the before-and-after behavior in routing tables and OSPF status output. As you study, keep in mind a key trade-off: summarization hides specifics and can prevent needless SPF recalculation, but summarizing too widely can create black holes if unreachable prefixes are included. Virtual links solve a special connectivity problem but add fragility and should be a last-resort design choice. By the end, you will be ready to configure area-range on an ABR and form a virtual link between ABRs with predictable verification steps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why OSPF route summarization matters, distinguish inter-area and external summarization, configure inter-area summarization on ABRs using Junos area-range, and describe both the purpose and caveats around virtual links. We start from practical goals: reduce routing table size, limit LSA flooding, and keep SPF runtimes reasonable. You will also learn the exact Junos commands for area-range on an ABR and for establishing a virtual link between two ABRs, including the requirement to use the other ABR's Router ID as the virtual-link neighbor. Finally, you will be able to verify both features with show commands and to recognize common mistakes: overly broad summaries that create black holes and virtual links that depend on a stable, standard transit area. These outcomes are operational: after studying, you should confidently configure area-range and a temporary virtual link in a lab and verify expected route advertisements.

screens.title: Why route summarization matters
screens.narratorSegment: Route summarization consolidates many specific prefixes into a single, broader prefix advertisement. Practically, that means fewer entries in routing tables on routers that don't need detail, less LSAs flooding across area boundaries, and fewer nodes recalculating SPF for changes that are local to a summarized block. For example, if Area 1 contains several /24 networks that share a contiguous /22 supernet, an ABR can advertise that /22 as a Type 3 LSA into Area 0. This reduces what remote routers store and how often they run SPF when one /24 flaps. A clear misconception to avoid is thinking summarization always preserves reachability visibility: overly broad summaries can create black holes if some specifics are not actually reachable. Summarization is most effective when you plan addressing to create contiguous blocks per area, so that summaries map cleanly to real reachability. In operational terms, summarization improves stability: when a specific link inside a summarized range goes down, the summary remains and prevents widespread SPF churn. Think of summarization as a local dampener for topology noise — valuable, but only when used with careful address planning. How might you apply this to an existing multi-area deployment?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Summarization aggregates specific routes into a broader advertisement to reduce state and LSA flooding.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Why summarization matters
What it is
Summarization replaces many specific routes with one broader route advertisement across area boundaries.
Benefits
  • Smaller routing tables on remote routers
  • Less LSA flooding between areas
  • Fewer SPF recalculations after local flaps
Common mistake
Summarize too broadly and you risk hiding unreachable specifics, creating traffic black holes.
Concrete example
Area 1 contains 172.16.1.0/24, .2.0/24, .3.0/24. These are contiguous and can be summarized as 172.16.0.0/22 for advertisement into Area 0.
Example Junos command
edit protocols ospf
set area 1.0.0.0 area-range 172.16.0.0/22
commit
Key Takeaway

Plan contiguous addressing per area before summarizing; use area-range on ABRs to export a single Type 3 summary.

Check your understanding
If a specific /24 inside the summary fails, will remote routers immediately lose reachability to the summarized block? Think about withdrawal behavior.

screens.title: Inter-area vs External summarization
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF supports two distinct summarization roles that serve different operational needs. Inter-area summarization happens on Area Border Routers and aggregates networks from one area before advertising them into another area, typically as Type 3 LSAs. This is the primary tool for multi-area OSPF: ABRs summarize internal area subnets to reduce state carried into the backbone or other areas. External summarization is performed by Autonomous System Boundary Routers when importing external routes into OSPF as Type 5 LSAs (or Type 7 for NSSA). That reduces the number of external prefixes advertised inside the OSPF domain. A common misconception is to treat both as equivalent; they are not. Inter-area summarization affects intra-OSPF area boundaries and is configured with area-range on ABRs, whereas external summarization condenses external learned routes on ASBRs before injection. An operational example: an ABR summarizing 172.16.0.0/22 for internal area networks, versus an ASBR aggregating external BGP prefixes into a single external advertisement. When verifying, use show route protocol ospf to see whether a summary Type 3 or a set of specifics is present, and inspect LSA types to confirm where the summary was generated. The takeaway: choose the appropriate summarization point based on the source of the routes and the scope you want to limit.

keyIdea.text: Inter-area summarization is an ABR action (Type 3); external summarization is done by ASBRs (Type 5/7) before injection.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Inter-area vs External
Inter-area summarization (ABR)
Aggregates internal area routes and advertises them into other areas as Type 3 LSAs. Configured on ABRs using area-range.
When to use
  • Multi-area designs with contiguous addressing
  • To protect backbone routers from internal detail
Risk
Poor address planning leads to black holes when specifics are not reachable.
External summarization (ASBR)
Aggregates routes learned from outside OSPF before injecting them as Type 5 LSAs (or Type 7 in NSSA). Done at the ASBR.
When to use
  • Importing many BGP prefixes into OSPF
  • Limit external LSA count inside OSPF domain
Operational check
Verify with LSA type inspection and show route protocol ospf to see whether summaries or specifics are present.
Key Takeaway

Summarize at the route source: ABR for intra-OSPF area content, ASBR for external imports.

Check
Which router created the summary? Inspect LSA types to confirm ABR vs ASBR origin.

screens.title: Configuring inter-area summarization on Junos
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through configuring inter-area summarization on a Juniper ABR. The command is straightforward: under protocols ospf you set area area-range on the ABR that connects the area with the specific subnets. This causes the ABR to advertise a Type 3 LSA for the summary to other areas. For example, summarizing 172.16.1.0/24,.2.0/24, and.3.0/24 into 172.16.0.0/22 is done with set area 1.0.0.0 area-range 172.16.0.0/22. After committing, the ABR generates a Type 3 LSA. A practical verification step is to run show route protocol ospf on a router in another area and confirm you see 172.16.0.0/22 instead of the three /24s. Misconceptions to avoid: the summary will be withdrawn if none of the specifics exist; area-range does not invent reachability. If you later add non-contiguous subnets, the summary may no longer represent accurate reachability. Use contiguous addressing and double-check with show route before and after the change to confirm behavior. Configuring inter-area summarization on Junos means use set area <id> area-range <summary/mask> under protocols ospf on the abr; it creates a type 3 summary lsa.. In practical terms, area-range on an abr and expected lsa behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Command
keyIdea.text: Use set area <id> area-range <summary/mask> under protocols ospf on the ABR; it creates a Type 3 summary LSA.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › area-range on ABR
Steps to configure
  1. Identify contiguous subnets inside an area suitable for summarization.
  2. On the ABR, under protocols ospf, set area area-range .
  3. Commit and verify with show route and LSA inspection.
Example
edit protocols ospf
set area 1.0.0.0 area-range 172.16.0.0/22
commit
Verification
Run show route protocol ospf on a router outside the summarized area. You should see the summary 172.16.0.0/22 advertised as a Type 3 route rather than the individual /24s.
Tip
If specifics disappear, the ABR withdraws the summary automatically. Use show route to confirm withdraw behavior when testing.
Pitfall
Do not summarize across unrelated addressing blocks; plan contiguous blocks per area.
Key Takeaway

area-range on ABRs is the operational control for inter-area summarization; verify with routing-table checks.

screens.title: How an ABR generates a Type 3 summary
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the lifecycle of a Type 3 summary helps prevent surprises. An ABR configured with area-range watches the specific routes within the source area. When at least one specific route that falls inside the configured summary exists, the ABR advertises the summary into other areas as a Type 3 LSA. If all of the finer-grained specifics disappear, the ABR withdraws the summary. This behavior means summaries are dynamic reflections of what the ABR sees inside the area, not static advertisements that persist regardless of reachability. A common operational misunderstanding is assuming the summary will keep traffic forwarding if all specifics are gone; in reality the summary will be withdrawn and reachability lost. For an example, configure area-range 172.16.0.0/22 on an ABR where the /24s exist. Pull one /24 down and watch SPF recalculation remain local; remove all /24s and the ABR withdraws the /22. Use show route and LSA interrogation to confirm the summary's presence and origin. This dynamic behavior is what makes summarization useful for containing instability, but also a reason to confirm contiguous addressing and availability before relying on summaries.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: A Type 3 summary is advertised while specifics exist; it is withdrawn when no specifics remain in the source area.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › ABR summary lifecycle
Step-by-step
1. Monitor specifics
ABR tracks specific routes that fall into the configured area-range.
2. Advertise summary
If any specific exists, ABR generates a Type 3 LSA for the summary.
3. Withdraw when empty
If no specifics remain, the ABR withdraws the summary automatically.
Example scenario
Area 1 has 172.16.1.0/24, .2.0/24, .3.0/24. ABR has area-range 172.16.0.0/22. Remove 172.16.2.0/24 and you still see the /22; remove all three and the /22 is withdrawn.
Verification commands
show route protocol ospf
show ospf database | match 172.16.0.0
Misconception
A summary persists regardless of specifics — false. It reflects current specifics.
Key Takeaway

Summaries are dynamic. Use verification after changes to confirm advertised state.

screens.title: What is a virtual link?
screens.narratorSegment: A virtual link is an OSPF mechanism that logically connects two Area Border Routers through a transit area so that a remote area can reach Area 0. It effectively extends Area 0 across that transit area by establishing a logical adjacency between the two ABRs using each other's Router ID as the neighbor identifier. Virtual links are used when an area cannot be attached directly to Area 0 due to topology constraints or design evolution. However, they are considered temporary and a last-resort measure because they introduce extra complexity and depend on the stability of the transit area. Important prerequisites for a virtual link to work include: the transit area must be a standard area (not stub, totally stubby, or NSSA), both ABRs must have interfaces in the transit area, and Router IDs used as neighbor-ids must be reachable via intra-area routes. A typical configuration is set area virtual-link neighbor-id. Remember: a virtual link does not replace good design. Treat it as a temporary bridge while a more stable backbone connection is planned. What is a virtual link? means a virtual link logically joins two abrs through a transit area so a disconnected area can reach area 0.. In practical terms, logical abr-to-abr connection that extends area 0 across a transit area. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A virtual link logically joins two ABRs through a transit area so a disconnected area can reach Area 0.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Virtual link definition
What it does
Creates a logical adjacency between two ABRs to present a remote area as connected to Area 0 through a transit area.
Use case
When an area is only connected to a non-backbone area and cannot be attached directly to Area 0.
Caveat
Virtual links are fragile: if the transit area path fails, the virtual link fails too.
Configuration pattern
# On ABR1
edit protocols ospf
set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 2.2.2.2
commit

# On ABR2
edit protocols ospf
set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 1.1.1.1
commit
Note: neighbor-id is the Router ID of the other ABR. The transit area must be a standard area connected to Area 0.
Key Takeaway

Virtual links are a last-resort logical extension of Area 0; verify transit area compatibility and Router ID reachability.

Misconfiguration checklist
  • Transit area must not be stub or NSSA.
  • Router IDs must be reachable inside the transit area.
  • Authentication must match if configured.

screens.title: Virtual link configuration example
screens.narratorSegment: Here's a concrete Junos example forming a virtual link between two ABRs, R1 and R2. Each ABR must be configured under the same transit area with the neighbor-id equal to the other ABR's Router ID. For instance, if R1 has Router ID 1.1.1.1 and R2 has Router ID 2.2.2.2, and the transit area is 5.0.0.0, configure R1 with set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 2.2.2.2 and R2 with set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 1.1.1.1. After committing, verify adjacency with show ospf neighbor and check the virtual-link status with show ospf virtual-link. The neighbor will appear in Full state when the virtual link is operational. A common troubleshooting point is reachability of the Router IDs: the transit area must provide intra-area reachability between the ABRs. If you see the virtual-link stuck in 2-way or not present, confirm interface area assignments, reachability of the Router IDs, and consistent authentication settings. Remember that a virtual link runs over the transit area's routed path — if that path flaps, the virtual link will flap too. Virtual link configuration example means set area <transit> virtual-link neighbor-id <other-abr-rid> on both abrs and verify with show ospf virtual-link.. In practical terms, forming a virtual link between two abrs in junos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: When to (and not to) use virtual links
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual links are useful when a remote area cannot directly attach to Area 0 and a temporary fix is needed to restore reachability. However, they add operational complexity and depend on the transit area's stability. Prefer a physical or logical redesign to attach the remote area directly to Area 0 when possible. Use virtual links for short-term migration, emergency recovery, or lab testing. A common misstep is to treat virtual links as permanent design: if the transit area becomes unstable, the virtual link will flap and routing may be unpredictable. Alternatives include readdressing to allow contiguous summarization, adding an actual link to Area 0, or redesigning area boundaries. Also note that the transit area must be a standard area; virtual links cannot traverse stub or NSSA areas. In practice, plan for monitoring and alerting on virtual-link status and keep authentication consistent across the transit area. Use the virtual link as a controlled, temporary bridge while you implement a more robust solution. When to (and not to) use virtual links means use virtual links only temporarily; prefer physical or addressing changes to restore backbone connectivity.. In practical terms, operational trade-offs and alternative solutions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn two scalable OSPF techniques: route summarization to keep routing tables compact and virtual links to temporarily reconnect an isolated area to the backbone. We'll show why summarization reduces memory and SPF work, how ABRs and ASBRs perform different summarization roles, and how a Junos ABR uses area-range to advertise a single Type 3 summary instead of multiple specific networks. Then we'll examine virtual links: what they are, when they are acceptable, and how to configure them by specifying the neighbor Router IDs and the transit area. You will see concrete Junos configuration examples and verification commands that demonstrate the before-and-after behavior in routing tables and OSPF status output. As you study, keep in mind a key trade-off: summarization hides specifics and can prevent needless SPF recalculation, but summarizing too widely can create black holes if unreachable prefixes are included. Virtual links solve a special connectivity problem but add fragility and should be a last-resort design choice. By the end, you will be ready to configure area-range on an ABR and form a virtual link between ABRs with predictable verification steps.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why OSPF route summarization matters, distinguish inter-area and external summarization, configure inter-area summarization on ABRs using Junos area-range, and describe both the purpose and caveats around virtual links. We start from practical goals: reduce routing table size, limit LSA flooding, and keep SPF runtimes reasonable. You will also learn the exact Junos commands for area-range on an ABR and for establishing a virtual link between two ABRs, including the requirement to use the other ABR's Router ID as the virtual-link neighbor. Finally, you will be able to verify both features with show commands and to recognize common mistakes: overly broad summaries that create black holes and virtual links that depend on a stable, standard transit area. These outcomes are operational: after studying, you should confidently configure area-range and a temporary virtual link in a lab and verify expected route advertisements.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills: crafting area-range commands for ABRs, creating virtual links with the correct neighbor Router IDs and transit area, and validating outcomes with show route and show ospf virtual-link. You will run commands that cause the ABR to generate Type 3 summary LSAs and you will observe how a summary remains when specifics fail within an area. For the virtual link, you'll ensure the transit area is a standard area and that reachability and authentication align. The learning outcomes emphasize not only command syntax but operational judgment: choose summarization masks that match contiguous addressing blocks, avoid summarizing across unrelated networks, and treat virtual links as temporary fixes. These applied objectives prepare you for the hands-on activity where you configure a virtual link between R2 and R3 and summarize two /24 networks into a single /23 on R3, then verify that upstream routers see the summary route.

Route summarization consolidates many specific prefixes into a single, broader prefix advertisement. Practically, that means fewer entries in routing tables on routers that don't need detail, less LSAs flooding across area boundaries, and fewer nodes recalculating SPF for changes that are local to a summarized block. For example, if Area 1 contains several /24 networks that share a contiguous /22 supernet, an ABR can advertise that /22 as a Type 3 LSA into Area 0. This reduces what remote routers store and how often they run SPF when one /24 flaps. A clear misconception to avoid is thinking summarization always preserves reachability visibility: overly broad summaries can create black holes if some specifics are not actually reachable. Summarization is most effective when you plan addressing to create contiguous blocks per area, so that summaries map cleanly to real reachability. In operational terms, summarization improves stability: when a specific link inside a summarized range goes down, the summary remains and prevents widespread SPF churn. Think of summarization as a local dampener for topology noise — valuable, but only when used with careful address planning. How might you apply this to an existing multi-area deployment?

OSPF supports two distinct summarization roles that serve different operational needs. Inter-area summarization happens on Area Border Routers and aggregates networks from one area before advertising them into another area, typically as Type 3 LSAs. This is the primary tool for multi-area OSPF: ABRs summarize internal area subnets to reduce state carried into the backbone or other areas. External summarization is performed by Autonomous System Boundary Routers when importing external routes into OSPF as Type 5 LSAs (or Type 7 for NSSA). That reduces the number of external prefixes advertised inside the OSPF domain. A common misconception is to treat both as equivalent; they are not. Inter-area summarization affects intra-OSPF area boundaries and is configured with area-range on ABRs, whereas external summarization condenses external learned routes on ASBRs before injection. An operational example: an ABR summarizing 172.16.0.0/22 for internal area networks, versus an ASBR aggregating external BGP prefixes into a single external advertisement. When verifying, use show route protocol ospf to see whether a summary Type 3 or a set of specifics is present, and inspect LSA types to confirm where the summary was generated. The takeaway: choose the appropriate summarization point based on the source of the routes and the scope you want to limit.

Let's walk through configuring inter-area summarization on a Juniper ABR. The command is straightforward: under protocols ospf you set area area-range on the ABR that connects the area with the specific subnets. This causes the ABR to advertise a Type 3 LSA for the summary to other areas. For example, summarizing 172.16.1.0/24,.2.0/24, and.3.0/24 into 172.16.0.0/22 is done with set area 1.0.0.0 area-range 172.16.0.0/22. After committing, the ABR generates a Type 3 LSA. A practical verification step is to run show route protocol ospf on a router in another area and confirm you see 172.16.0.0/22 instead of the three /24s. Misconceptions to avoid: the summary will be withdrawn if none of the specifics exist; area-range does not invent reachability. If you later add non-contiguous subnets, the summary may no longer represent accurate reachability. Use contiguous addressing and double-check with show route before and after the change to confirm behavior. Configuring inter-area summarization on Junos means use set area <id> area-range <summary/mask> under protocols ospf on the abr; it creates a type 3 summary lsa.. In practical terms, area-range on an abr and expected lsa behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the lifecycle of a Type 3 summary helps prevent surprises. An ABR configured with area-range watches the specific routes within the source area. When at least one specific route that falls inside the configured summary exists, the ABR advertises the summary into other areas as a Type 3 LSA. If all of the finer-grained specifics disappear, the ABR withdraws the summary. This behavior means summaries are dynamic reflections of what the ABR sees inside the area, not static advertisements that persist regardless of reachability. A common operational misunderstanding is assuming the summary will keep traffic forwarding if all specifics are gone; in reality the summary will be withdrawn and reachability lost. For an example, configure area-range 172.16.0.0/22 on an ABR where the /24s exist. Pull one /24 down and watch SPF recalculation remain local; remove all /24s and the ABR withdraws the /22. Use show route and LSA interrogation to confirm the summary's presence and origin. This dynamic behavior is what makes summarization useful for containing instability, but also a reason to confirm contiguous addressing and availability before relying on summaries.

A virtual link is an OSPF mechanism that logically connects two Area Border Routers through a transit area so that a remote area can reach Area 0. It effectively extends Area 0 across that transit area by establishing a logical adjacency between the two ABRs using each other's Router ID as the neighbor identifier. Virtual links are used when an area cannot be attached directly to Area 0 due to topology constraints or design evolution. However, they are considered temporary and a last-resort measure because they introduce extra complexity and depend on the stability of the transit area. Important prerequisites for a virtual link to work include: the transit area must be a standard area (not stub, totally stubby, or NSSA), both ABRs must have interfaces in the transit area, and Router IDs used as neighbor-ids must be reachable via intra-area routes. A typical configuration is set area virtual-link neighbor-id. Remember: a virtual link does not replace good design. Treat it as a temporary bridge while a more stable backbone connection is planned. What is a virtual link? means a virtual link logically joins two abrs through a transit area so a disconnected area can reach area 0.. Here's a concrete Junos example forming a virtual link between two ABRs, R1 and R2. Each ABR must be configured under the same transit area with the neighbor-id equal to the other ABR's Router ID. For instance, if R1 has Router ID 1.1.1.1 and R2 has Router ID 2.2.2.2, and the transit area is 5.0.0.0, configure R1 with set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 2.2.2.2 and R2 with set area 5.0.0.0 virtual-link neighbor-id 1.1.1.1. After committing, verify adjacency with show ospf neighbor and check the virtual-link status with show ospf virtual-link. The neighbor will appear in Full state when the virtual link is operational. A common troubleshooting point is reachability of the Router IDs: the transit area must provide intra-area reachability between the ABRs. If you see the virtual-link stuck in 2-way or not present, confirm interface area assignments, reachability of the Router IDs, and consistent authentication settings. Remember that a virtual link runs over the transit area's routed path — if that path flaps, the virtual link will flap too. Virtual link configuration example means set area <transit> virtual-link neighbor-id <other-abr-rid> on both abrs and verify with show ospf virtual-link.. Virtual links are useful when a remote area cannot directly attach to Area 0 and a temporary fix is needed to restore reachability. However, they add operational complexity and depend on the transit area's stability. Prefer a physical or logical redesign to attach the remote area directly to Area 0 when possible. Use virtual links for short-term migration, emergency recovery, or lab testing. A common misstep is to treat virtual links as permanent design: if the transit area becomes unstable, the virtual link will flap and routing may be unpredictable. Alternatives include readdressing to allow contiguous summarization, adding an actual link to Area 0, or redesigning area boundaries. Also note that the transit area must be a standard area; virtual links cannot traverse stub or NSSA areas. In practice, plan for monitoring and alerting on virtual-link status and keep authentication consistent across the transit area. Use the virtual link as a controlled, temporary bridge while you implement a more robust solution. Let's summarize the most important ideas. First: route summarization aggregates multiple specific routes into a single advertisement to reduce routing table size and limit LSA flooding — use contiguous addressing per area to avoid black holes. Second: inter-area summarization occurs on ABRs and creates Type 3 LSAs when you configure area-range; it is the right tool to reduce intra-OSPF detail across areas. Third: external summarization happens on ASBRs when importing routes from other protocols and is used to limit the number of external LSAs. Keep these distinctions clear when you design summarization: summarize at the source and verify with show route and LSA inspection to confirm where summaries originate.
